title: Twenty-one years at the Celebrity Club, 1950 to 1971
summary: Tate describes the size of the band, the book, and how rock and disco ended the job.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well, I only had seven and with a singer, made eight. But you know, we had a minimum. Sometime I'd have to augment the band to twelve and twelve to fifteen pieces. So I had my book written for that. They all, you know, took time and they, you know, wrote arrangements for -- so I always had a book for those guys to, you know, to play. And that's how the band really -- for 21 years, man, we worked the Celebrity Club and we didn't get fired, we just quit, because he started catering to all rock and we'd play sometime and this kid would stand against the wall and look at us, say, 'Are they crazy?' You know, because we weren't playing like -- we weren't playing that -- what they really wanted. So then Eli started writing arrangements, the same tunes, but then the cats wanted us to sing like James Brown, you know? They wanted -- so --
So you were there from '50 to '71.
That was a hell of a long period.
That's a hell of a long gig, man.
How did you keep replenishing the book?
Well, we kept writing, kept writing and

listening, you know, and things like that. And I tell you, it wasn't until the last -- I'd say the last two years before the -- all the other times, we were just tops. But in the last two years, when the kids started coming in, you know, like disco now, this -- they want it all hard rock and they wanted James Brown things. So --
